opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to recognize is that the core ideas carry over really well, but the setting is quite different from the one we were working in with games. With AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero, you had a perfect environment. You had a simulator, you had a clear reward at the end of the game, win or lose, and you could play millions of games against yourself. The reward signal was clean and it was grounded in something real.

With language models, the hardest part isn't really the algorithm. It's the reward. In most real-world tasks there's no ground-truth signal telling you whether a response was good. So early on, the field relied heavily on learned reward models from human preferences, which is RLHF. That works surprisingly well for making models more helpful and aligned with what people want, but a learned reward model is something the policy can exploit. If you optimize against it too hard, you get reward hacking, and the model finds strange ways to look good without actually being good.

What's exciting now is that we're finding more domains where you do have something closer to a verifiable reward: math, where you can check the answer, code, where you can run tests, and more broadly agentic tasks, where you can see whether the task actually got done. In those settings, RL starts to look a lot more like what we did in games. You can let the model try many times, explore different reasoning paths, and reinforce what actually works. That's where you see behaviors emerge that nobody explicitly taught: the model backtracks, checks its work, tries a different approach.

The other big difference is the starting point. In AlphaZero we started from scratch, tabula rasa. With language models you start from an incredibly strong prior from pretraining. That changes everything about exploration. You're not searching randomly; you're searching in the space of things a very knowledgeable model already considers plausible. So RL here is less about discovering knowledge from nothing and more about sharpening and eliciting capabilities, teaching the model how to use what it already knows to reason over longer horizons.

So my view is that the principles — search, self-improvement, learning from experience — are the same. The open research questions are about building better environments and better reward signals, especially for tasks that aren't easily verifiable. That's where I think a lot of the next progress will come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, because on the surface RL for language models looks very different from the settings I came from, like Atari or Go, but underneath, the core ideas carry over surprisingly well.

The way I frame it is: reinforcement learning is fundamentally about learning from feedback that's sparser and noisier than a supervised label. In Go, you play a whole game and only at the end do you find out whether you won. With a language model, you generate a long response, maybe a multi-step reasoning chain, and you only get a signal at the end about whether it was correct or whether a human preferred it. That's the same credit assignment problem. Which tokens, which decisions along the way, actually mattered?

What's different is the starting point. In AlphaGo, we started from a policy trained on human games, and then self-play took it far beyond that. With language models, you start from a pretrained model that's already an extraordinarily strong prior. So RL isn't building capability from scratch, it's shaping and sharpening what's already there. That changes a lot of practical decisions. You care enormously about not drifting too far from the base model, because the base model is where most of the knowledge lives. That's why you see things like KL penalties and relatively conservative updates. In games, we were happy to let the policy wander wherever the reward took it.

The second big difference is the reward. In Go, the reward is perfectly defined. There's no ambiguity about who won. For language, the reward is either a learned model of human preferences, which can be gamed, or some verifiable signal like a math answer matching or a unit test passing. I'm much more optimistic about the verifiable domains, because that's where RL historically shines. When the reward is clean, the model can explore, try unusual strategies, and you'll see genuinely new behavior emerge, like the longer, more deliberate reasoning that's come out of the recent reasoning models. When the reward is a learned proxy, you're always in a bit of an arms race with reward hacking, and you have to be humble about that.

The third thing, which I find the most interesting, is search. A lot of what made our game-playing systems work was combining learning with search at test time, with the model's intuition guiding the search and the search improving the model. With language models, the analog is spending more compute at inference, sampling multiple attempts, verifying, and then distilling that back into training. I think we're still early on the right way to do that for open-ended tasks, but the loop of "think harder at test time, then learn from what the thinking found" is the same loop that got us from AlphaGo to AlphaZero.

So my honest summary is: the algorithms are more similar than people expect, but the engineering judgment is different. You're working with an expensive prior you don't want to break, rewards you can't fully trust, and a much broader action space. The art is in respecting those constraints while still letting the model actually discover something.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to view the language model as a policy. It generates tokens, those tokens lead to an answer or an action, and reinforcement learning gives us a way to improve that behavior based on the outcome.

But the difficult question is: what outcome do you reward? If you're solving a problem where you can check the answer, you have a fairly clear signal. If you're trying to produce a helpful response to an open-ended question, defining that signal is much harder. You can use human feedback, but you have to be careful that optimizing the feedback actually improves the behavior you care about.

The other important difference is that you're starting with a pretrained model that already has substantial capabilities. So you're not learning everything from scratch. You're using reinforcement learning to help the model make better use of what it has learned—and, with enough exploration and reliable feedback, discover better ways of solving problems.

r002.rationale: It does not describe training the policy to imitate possibilities selected through planning.

r003.rationale: It mentions human feedback, but not using an LLM’s feedback on its own output instead of a value network to evaluate candidate outputs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to recognize that you’re starting from a model that already has a very rich set of capabilities from pretraining. So reinforcement learning isn’t learning everything from scratch. It’s shaping how the model uses those capabilities to solve a task.

You can think of generating a response as a sequence of actions, where each action is a token. The challenge is deciding what to reward. For something like a mathematical problem, you may be able to check the final answer. For a more open-ended conversation, defining success is much harder, and you might need human feedback or a learned reward model.

Then there’s exploration and credit assignment. If a model produces a long solution and gets the answer wrong, which decisions should change? And how do you encourage it to discover a better approach rather than just reinforce what it already tends to do?

So the underlying reinforcement learning ideas still apply, but the starting point, the scale, and the way we specify rewards change quite a lot.
